passage: Dear Sanna, the allotment committee has spoken, and we have lost the water argument but won the shed one, which on reflection is the better half of the bargain. From April the standpipes will run only on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, a rationing the committee blames on last summer's bill of 2,100 dollars, of which, the treasurer let slip, fully a third was one man's sprinkler running nights on plot 40; he has been spoken to, and has resigned in a huff, and his gooseberries will be missed if he is not. The shed victory: we may now build to eight feet at the ridge instead of six, which means Viktor's salvaged windows will fit after all, and the greenhouse-shed we drew on the back of the seed catalogue in February can go ahead. I have paid our plot fee, 85 dollars, and put us down for two barrels of the municipal leaf mold at 10 dollars the barrel, which sells out by March, so thank me later. The rhubarb is already showing, three weeks early, and old Mrs. Egger prophesies a hard April in consequence; she is usually right, so keep the fleece handy and do not let your courgettes flatter you into planting out before the frosts are done. Yours in mud, Berit.
question: On which days will the standpipes run from April?

passage: Dear Aldous, you asked for the story of the sourdough starter now that it has passed to you, and a starter without its story is just gray paste, so here it is. It began, as far as anyone can prove, in my grandmother's kitchen in the winter of 1954, though she claimed descent from her own aunt's crock, unverifiable, and the family lets the claim stand out of respect. It has crossed the country four times, survived a house fire in 1978 riding in the milk crate that was all my mother grabbed besides the photographs, and endured eleven months of neglect in the back of my refrigerator during the year of the divorce, from which it revived in three days, which is more than I can say for myself. Feed it by weight, not volume: 100 grams of flour, 100 of water, once a week in the cold months and twice in summer, and always after it doubles, never by the clock alone. It likes rye but does not need it. If the gray liquor forms on top, stir it back in; that is its complaining, not its dying. And when your daughter is older, split it and hand it on with this letter copied out in your own hand, which is the actual recipe. Yours, Marek.
question: In what winter did the starter begin, as far as anyone can prove?

passage: Dear Ines, I promised you the truth about the walking holiday, and here it is, with the blisters still voting. The route notes called the third day moderate, which we now know is a term of art meaning nine hours, two of them lost above the tree line in cloud following cairns that a poet, not a surveyor, had spaced. Hedda was magnificent and insufferable, having trained all spring as threatened, and she reached the refuge a full hour before me, where she had the grace to order my soup and the cruelty to time me from the doorway. The refuge itself redeemed everything: forty bunks, a stove like a ship's boiler, and a warden who has kept the mountain book for 34 years and read us the entry from the night of the great storm as though it were scripture. I bathed my feet in the snowmelt trough with a Belgian schoolteacher and a shepherd, all of us hissing in three languages. Day four we came down through the larch woods singing, which I deny in advance if quoted. Total: 62 miles, one lost hat, no regrets. Next year the coast path, which the notes call gentle, a word I no longer trust. Come with us and bring better socks than I did. Love, Vera.
question: How long had the warden kept the mountain book?

passage: Dear Mr. Standish, my grandfather, Arne Lindqvist, worked at your family's boatyard from 1946 until it closed in 1969, and I am writing on the long chance that your records survive. He died in January, at 96, and among his things we found a brass half model of a hull, marked on the back with the number 118 and the letters VS, which my mother believes stands for the yard, Viksund and Standish, as it was then. He spoke rarely of those years, but when he did it was of one boat, a pilot cutter he called the proud one, whose sea trials he described to my brother the week before he died with a clarity he no longer had for breakfast. We would dearly like to know whether hull 118 was that cutter, what she was named at launch, and whether she survives anywhere, even as a wreck or a photograph. I enclose a photograph of the half model and stamped return postage, and I apologize for asking you to dig through what may be seventy years of dust for a stranger. If the records burned or were lost, a line saying so would still be an answer, and would be received with gratitude. Respectfully, Johan Lindqvist.
question: What number is marked on the back of the brass half model?

passage: Dearest Franka, the exam results came Thursday, and I have made you wait until I could write calmly, which took until Sunday. I passed. All four papers, including pharmacology, which you will remember I sat with a fever in March and left convinced I had confused two drug families for an entire essay; it turns out I had, and the examiners noted it, and passed me anyway on the strength of the rest, with a comment about sound reasoning from a wrong premise that I intend to have framed. So your little sister is, from the first of September, a qualified veterinary nurse, with a post already offered at the Bramwell clinic, the small one by the level crossing, three days a week to start and full time when Mrs. Ostrander retires at Christmas. The wage is nothing to sing about, 2,200 a month before deductions, but the head vet is the woman who let me observe the colic surgery when I was seventeen and wavering, and I would honestly work for her in exchange for sandwiches. Papa cried, denies it, and has told the entire street. Mama has moved from open opposition to claiming the idea as hers, which we agreed is her way of blessing it. Come home for the first weekend of September and we will celebrate properly. Your Mia.
question: At which clinic has the writer been offered a post?

passage: Dear Neighbor, an introduction and a confession together, since we have waved across the lane for a month without proper names: I am Edda Kryger, at the gray house with the crooked chimney, and it was my goat, not the wind, that opened your gate on Tuesday and pruned your roses to the height of a goat. Her name is Duchess, she opens simple latches with her lips, a skill we discovered too late to unteach, and she has a criminal record in three gardens already. I am sorrier than this cheerful paragraph sounds. By way of amends you will find on your step a jar of quince jelly, a round of our own cheese, and a voucher of my own invention promising one full day of my labor in your garden at any date you name, which I suggest you spend on the fence between us; I will supply the wire. My husband proposes instead that we simply give you the goat, but he proposes this to everyone and no one has ever accepted. Should you see her again on your side, do not chase her, she thinks it is a game and she is faster than you; rattle the feed bucket, which is by our gate, and she will betray her freedom instantly for oats. Welcome to the lane. Yours, in embarrassment, Edda.
question: What is the goat's name?

passage: Dear Halvor, the band needs to decide about the festival, and since you are the only one whose head works in lists, here is the situation in one letter. The offer: the second stage at Grenfell Hollow, the Saturday, a 40 minute set at five in the afternoon, fee of 600 dollars against, and this is the catch, our own travel, and the van's gearbox has been making its views known since the wedding in April. Miri can borrow her brother's horse trailer, cleaned, she claims, but that means towing with her old estate car, and the pass road with a trailer is nobody's idea of a joke. The alternative is the early train, instruments as luggage, which the festival says worked for the Tullamore fiddlers last year, though they travel lighter than we do by one double bass, and Osric refuses to discuss shipping the bass ahead after what the couriers did to his amplifier in the winter, which to be fair to him still buzzes on one string of the low E. My vote: train, bass and all, one porter's trolley, and we pocket the difference toward the gearbox. Ring me Thursday; the festival wants an answer by the 14th, and if we say yes, rehearsals go to twice a week, no exceptions, including you, fisherman. Yours, Grete.
question: What fee has the festival offered?

passage: Dear Mrs. Alberdine, I taught your daughter Sophie in the fourth class this year, and school reports being the corseted things they are, I am writing you a letter besides, which I do for one or two children a year and always in July, when no one can mistake it for procedure. The report says Sophie meets expectations in mathematics, which is true and useless. What the boxes cannot hold: in October, when we did the unit on measurement, Sophie decided the classroom's published floor area was wrong, remeasured it during three lunch breaks with the caretaker's tape, found the plan had ignored the bay window, and submitted a correction of 4.2 square meters with a drawing, to the school office, in an envelope, addressed to whom it may concern. The office wrote back. She has the file. I tell you this because that particular stubbornness, the kind that checks the official number, does not always survive school, and it is worth protecting even when it is inconvenient, which at home I imagine is often. She should meet a surveyor, or an auditor, or a physicist, whichever your acquaintance runs to; she does not yet know these are jobs. I enclose her drawing, having kept a photocopy for myself, frankly, as encouragement in dull terms. Kind regards, T. Weiss.
question: By how much did Sophie find the published floor area to be wrong?

passage: Dear Bruno, the apple pressing is set for the second Saturday of October, and this year we are organized, by which I mean I am writing to you in August instead of ringing you the night before. The press is booked from the cooperative, the big twin basket one, for the whole day at 45 dollars, and Merle has promised her trailer for collecting the crates from the three gardens on Friday evening, yours last because of the hill. Bring what you have, but the Kohlmann sisters have already declared a glut, their trees having gone mad in alternation as usual, so we will not starve; last year we pressed 380 liters between eleven households and the record, 2019, stands at 520. Jobs: you are on the mill again, by acclamation, because you are the only one who feeds it steadily instead of in guilty avalanches, and your Lotte, if she will, runs the label table for the children, whose bottles from last year, the ones with the potato print stars, people actually fought over. Bottles washed and brought by nine, sterilizing tubs on the fire by half past, first juice by eleven if the weather holds. If it rains we squeeze into the Vogel barn as before and complain, which is also traditional. No need to reply unless you cannot come, in which case reply, and reconsider. Yours, Anselm.
question: How many liters were pressed last year?

passage: My dear Corinna, you asked how the shop is faring in its second year, and because you were the one who talked me out of quitting in the first winter, you get the true ledger, not the market day smile. We are, by a whisker, profitable: eleven months of the last twelve in the black, the exception being February, which is February. The wholesale account with the two cafes in Dunning came good, and their standing order, 40 loaves and 60 rolls thrice weekly, is the spine the whole week hangs on; walk-in trade still swings with the weather like a barometer. I have hired help at last, mornings only, a retired ships cook named Abel who kneads like a man settling an old score and has quietly fixed my rye, which I will admit to you and deny at the counter, was never quite right before him. The oven's middle deck died in June, 900 dollars, which ate the summer's margin, and the landlord hints at a rent review in spring, so I am not ordering the awning yet. But Corinna, on Saturdays there is a queue before I unbolt the door, and old Mr. Fenwick told me the smell reaches the war memorial when the wind sits right, and he counts this among the town's improvements. We are all right. Come and see us. Flour everywhere, Paulina.
question: What is the name of the retired ships cook hired for mornings?
